capability_investigated:
The fixed 30s/3000-frame mel produced by WhisperProcessor's feature
extractor, and generate()'s acceptance of a batched features tensor with a
per-item prompt list (not just a single window).
what_i_learned:
The stub's single processor(audio) call truncates every clip to 30s, so all
audio past 0:30 is silently dropped before decode — the dominant deletion
source on long 0715 calls. generate() takes [N,128,3000] batched features
with N prompts, so multiple windows decode in one call within budget.
hypothesis:
Split audio into 30s windows, extract each to its own mel, batch-decode them
in a single generate() call, and join the per-window transcripts in order to
recover the truncated tail and lower deletion-driven CER.

capability_investigated:
generate()'s memory behavior when handed a batched [N,128,3000] features
tensor — specifically how N (window count) scales VRAM, since the parent
passed every 30s window of a minutes-long call in one call.
what_i_learned:
generate() accepts arbitrarily many batched windows API-wise, but the
single-call form is not memory-safe: a full minutes-long call produces
enough 30s windows that one [N,128,3000] decode exhausts CUDA memory
(RuntimeError: out of memory). Peak VRAM scales with N, so N must be
capped — the batched call has a memory ceiling the API does not enforce.
hypothesis:
Keep 30s windowing (fixes the 0:30 truncation / deletion source) but decode
in fixed-size sub-batches of 4 windows per generate() call, bounding peak
memory independent of clip length. This should run to completion and score
instead of OOM-crashing the evaluator.

capability_investigated:
generate()'s **decoding_kwargs beyond beam_size/sampling_temperature — the
ctranslate2 Whisper beam-search controls the parent never set: patience,
length_penalty (length normalization exponent), and no_repeat_ngram_size.
what_i_learned:
The parent decodes every 30s window with beam_size=1 (pure greedy) and only
sampling_temperature=0.0, leaving the whole beam-search surface unused. ct2's
generate accepts patience, length_penalty and no_repeat_ngram_size on the same
call; length_penalty normalizes the beam score by pow(len, lp), so lp>1 rewards
longer sequences — a knob aimed straight at the deletion/coverage axis that
greedy decode cannot reach. Deletion (80%) and length_ratio ~0.65 are uniform
across files, not just repeated_text ones, so undergeneration is systematic.
hypothesis:
Replace greedy per-window decode with tuned beam search (beam_size=5,
patience=2.0, length_penalty=1.1, no_repeat_ngram_size=3). Wider beam + patience
recover content that greedy drops via early EOS on quiet/noisy windows,
length_penalty>1 favors longer hypotheses to raise length_ratio toward 1.0, and
no_repeat_ngram_size=3 suppresses the repetition collapse flagged as
repeated_text — all targeting the dominant coverage/deletion axis.

capability_investigated:
generate()'s decode-prompt control over timestamp emission, and the timestamp
tokens that appear inside results[0].sequences_ids when <|notimestamps|> is
absent — information the pipeline currently discards via skip_special_tokens.
what_i_learned:
The prompt list fully controls timestamp mode: omitting <|notimestamps|> makes
the model emit <|t.tt|> segment-timestamp tokens (ids >= the <|0.00|> token id)
interleaved in sequences_ids, each encoding time = (id - ts_begin) * 0.02 s
relative to the window start. This exposes WHERE each decoded segment ends —
enabling reference-style seeking instead of fixed 30s hops. It is reachable
through the frozen surface with no new import.
hypothesis:
Deletion is concentrated at the hard 30s cuts that slice utterances the model
then can't reconstruct. Decode each window with timestamps on, keep text only
up to the last segment-end timestamp, and advance the next window's start to
that time — windows snap to segment boundaries so no utterance is sliced and
no overlap is duplicated, lifting length_ratio against the coverage axis.

capability_investigated:
The `prompts` argument to generate() — not its decode kwargs but the token
prefix itself. Whisper's prompt accepts a previous-text conditioning block
(<|startofprev|> + prior text token ids) placed BEFORE the
<|startoftranscript|> SOT sequence; the pipeline has only ever passed the
bare 4-token SOT sequence.
what_i_learned:
generate()'s per-item prompt can encode condition_on_previous_text: prepending
<|startofprev|> + recent text token ids (those with id < the <|endoftext|> id,
i.e. non-special text tokens) to the SOT suffix is accepted by the same
batched call with no new import and no extra VRAM (encoder features unchanged,
only the prompt grows). This is an input axis distinct from the timestamp
OUTPUT probe in iter_004 — prompt-prefix conditioning, never used before.
hypothesis:
Fixed 30s windows decode each batch as a cold start from silence, dropping the
leading partial utterance at every boundary — a uniform deletion source
matching del 77% / len 0.71. Carrying the previous batch's decoded text as a
<|startofprev|> prompt prefix (capped at 200 text tokens) primes the model
across boundaries, recovering boundary-cut content and raising length_ratio
without changing the batched-decode memory ceiling.

capability_investigated:
generate()'s decoder KV-cache memory scaling under prev-text prompt
conditioning: how peak VRAM depends on (window-batch x beam x prompt+gen
seq_len) once <|startofprev|>+prev_tokens is prepended to the SOT suffix.
what_i_learned:
iter_005's OOM was not from the encoder (features stay [N,128,3000]) but from
the decoder: prepending ~200 prev-text tokens lengthens every beam sequence,
and at batch=4 x beam=5 = 20 concurrent sequences that pushed the KV-cache
past VRAM. Peak decoder memory ~ batch x beam x seq_len, so halving the window
batch (10 sequences) more than offsets the longer prompt — below iter_003's
working 20-sequence footprint. Prompt growth is a memory axis distinct from
window count (iter_002's finding).
hypothesis:
Keep iter_005's previous-text conditioning (cross-window context to recover
boundary deletions) but set _BATCH_WINDOWS=2 and _PREV_CONTEXT_TOKENS=100 so
the longer prompts stay within the VRAM ceiling, letting the conditioning
actually be evaluated against the coverage axis.

capability_investigated:
generate()'s peak decoder VRAM as a joint function of windows-per-call and
prev-text prompt length — combining iter_002's window-count memory axis with
iter_006's prompt-growth axis on the same call, rather than treating them
separately.
what_i_learned:
iter_006 OOM'd at batch=2 despite halving the window batch, which means
halving the window-count lever alone does not get the longer-prompt KV-cache
under the ceiling — peak ~ windows x beam x (prev+gen) seq_len, so both
multipliers must drop together. Decoding one window per generate call makes
concurrency exactly 1 x beam, the minimum reachable while keeping beam search,
and is also the natural form for prev-text since each prefix depends on the
prior window's emitted tokens; the per-call features stay [1,128,3000].
hypothesis:
Keep iter_003's beam-search coverage settings and iter_005's prev-text
conditioning, but eliminate the OOM by setting windows-per-call to 1 and
trimming the prev-context block to 64 tokens, so peak decoder memory is far
below iter_003's working footprint and the candidate actually scores.

capability_investigated:
How the windowing geometry (start stride vs window length) interacts with the
two parents' decode paths — specifically what happens to speech that straddles
a non-overlapping 30s seam, and whether overlapping the windows + a stitch-time
dedup can recover that span without re-importing anything or growing per-call
VRAM (each window stays a single [1,128,3000] generate call).
what_i_learned:
Both parent families stall on the identical axis (deletion 0.76, length_ratio
0.71) regardless of beam search (family_001) or prev-text conditioning
(family_003) — so the residual coverage loss is not a decode-knob problem but a
geometry one: the fixed non-overlapping 30s stride cuts words/segments at every
seam, and neither the window that ends mid-word nor the one that starts mid-word
recovers the fragment. The stride is independent of the window length: stepping
by 26s while still extracting a 30s mel makes every seam doubly covered at the
cost of ~15% more single-window calls, which stays inside the 719s budget. This
is a chunking lever distinct from every decode-kwarg in the ledger.
hypothesis:
Graft family_003's prev-text+single-window decode and family_001's beam search
(already shared) and add the missing deletion guard: overlap windows (4s) and
dedup the doubly-covered text by removing the largest leading word run of each
new piece that exactly re-states the trailing words of the accumulator. Seam
speech is now transcribed by a window that contains it whole, lifting coverage
on the dominant deletion axis, while the exact-match word dedup prevents the
overlap from regressing the hallucination/insertion axis family_001 lost on.

capability_investigated:
The decode-kwarg set on generate() — specifically no_repeat_ngram_size=3,
one of four beam-search overrides the combine pipeline carries, checked
against the observed repeated_text rate it is supposed to guard.
what_i_learned:
no_repeat_ngram_size=3 is a repetition guard, but the best candidate's
error profile shows repeated 0.00 across the batch — there is no repetition
for trigram-blocking to suppress, so this knob is plausibly inert on the
0715 calls. The remaining beam surface (beam_size, patience, length_penalty)
is what acts on the deletion/coverage axis; the ngram guard is orthogonal to
it. This ablation tests whether the guard is load-bearing or dead weight.
hypothesis:
Drop no_repeat_ngram_size=3 from the single-window generate call. If CER
holds (repeated stays 0.00), the simpler decode is the win — fewer beam
constraints, marginally faster, and one less knob to reason about; if
repetition reappears, the guard was load-bearing and the next iter restores it.

capability_investigated:
generate()'s decoded OUTPUT under a timestamp-enabled SOT prompt — the
<|t.tt|> segment-timestamp tokens (id >= <|0.00|> id) that appear in
results[0].sequences_ids when <|notimestamps|> is omitted, and using the
LAST such token to drive the next window's start instead of a fixed stride.
what_i_learned:
The fixed-hop deletion is an early-termination artifact: the decoder emits
<|endoftext|> before the 30s mel is exhausted, so a constant stride steps
past speech it never committed to. The last emitted segment timestamp gives
the reliable decode boundary per window (time = (id - ts_begin) * 0.02 s),
letting the window start track the audio adaptively — the un-decoded tail is
re-seeked, not dropped. This consumes iter_004's timestamp finding, which had
been measured but never used for seeking.
hypothesis:
Replacing the fixed/overlap stride with timestamp-driven seeking (advance to
last segment-end ts, floored by _MIN_ADVANCE_SECONDS=15 to bound window count
and guard degenerate windows) recovers the deletion that every fixed-hop diff
left on the floor, raising length_ratio toward 1.0 while prev-text + dedup
hold hallucination/insertion in place.
